title: Composting horse manure and straw bedding
subtitle: Hot composting stable waste into usable garden compost over 3 to 6 months
excerpt: Horse manure mixed with straw bedding is one of the best materials for hot composting. The straw provides carbon structure and aeration; the manure provides nitrogen and microbial inoculant. A well-built horse manure heap reaches 55 to 70°C within days and produces finished compost in 3 to 6 months with turning.
sourceNotes: WRAP (Waste and Resources Action Programme) guidance on composting horse manure. RHS guidance on using stable manure in the garden. Cornell Composting Science and Engineering guide on livestock manure (public domain, Cornell University Extension). Horse manure C:N ratio data from ADAS soils laboratory guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: The ratio of carbon to nitrogen in organic material. Horse manure with straw has a C:N ratio of around 25:1, close to the ideal composting range of 20:30:1.
A composting method that builds a large heap with a C:N ratio close to 25:1, achieving temperatures of 55 to 70°C that kill weed seeds and pathogens.

content.text: Horse manure fresh from the stable has a
C:N ratio
of around 20 to 30:1 depending on the straw content. This is close to the ideal range for
hot composting
. A heap built from mixed stable waste reaches 55°C or above within 2 to 5 days if the pile is large enough (at least 1 cubic metre) and moist enough.

attrs.title: Safety: composting preamble
attrs.body: Garden gloves at minimum. A well-rotted manure heap is mostly bacterial fungi and earthworms; the fresh layer can carry sharp straw ends, broken glass from yard sweepings, and the occasional rusty staple. Long sleeves if you are sensitive to mould spore.

content.text: What makes horse manure different from other composts

Horse manure is weed-seed rich. The gut of a horse does not fully kill grass and weed seeds. A hot composting process with sustained temperatures above 55°C kills seeds within a week. Cold or lukewarm composting will create a weed-laden soil amendment.

Wood-shaving bedding composting is slower than straw. Wood shavings have a C:N ratio of around 500:1 and may need 12 to 18 months to break down fully, or the addition of a nitrogen source (chicken manure, ammonium sulphate).
Fresh horse manure applied directly to vegetable beds risks burning seedlings from ammonia release and may transmit antibiotic residues from medicated horses. Composting removes both risks.
Building and managing the heap
Build the heap at least 1 m x 1 m x 1 m. Below this size it loses heat too quickly. 1.5 m x 1.5 m x 1.5 m is better for sustained temperature.
Add equal volumes of straw and manure in alternating 150 mm layers if they are not pre-mixed in the stable.
Check moisture: the heap should feel like a wrung-out sponge. Dry heaps do not heat; wet heaps smell and go anaerobic. Add water if the manure is dry.
Take temperature readings with a compost thermometer at 200 mm depth after 48 hours. The heap should be at 45°C or above. If not, turn the outer layers into the centre.

Turn the heap when the temperature falls below 45°C (typically every 5 to 10 days in the first month). Move the outer material to the centre. The heap will re-heat within 24 hours if it is not too wet or too dry.
Weed seed kill check

For weed seed kill, the whole heap must reach 55°C for at least 3 consecutive days. The outer edges do not reach this temperature without turning. A three-turn protocol, each time moving the outer material into the centre, ensures every part of the heap has had at least one period in the hot zone.
When it is ready

After 3 to 6 months, finished horse compost is dark brown, crumbly, and smells of earth. No straw strands are visible. Weed seeds in a small test sample placed on damp compost do not germinate within a week. Apply at 5 to 10 litres per m² as a surface mulch or dig in to 150 mm depth.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Heap smells of ammonia after building
rows.cause: Too much nitrogen (heavily soiled manure) relative to carbon from straw, or heap too wet
rows.fix: Add a 150 mm layer of dry straw or cardboard to absorb ammonia and adjust the C:N ratio. Cover the heap to reduce further wetting.

rows.symptom: Heap does not heat above 30°C despite being large enough
rows.cause: Too dry, or wood-shaving bedding with a very high C:N ratio
rows.fix: Water the heap slowly from the top. For wood-shaving bedding, add a nitrogen source such as fresh grass clippings or a nitrogen fertiliser at 50 g/m².
